result:
**Solution A is invalid.** Its construction has covering number at most k−1, not k. Each B_j has k−1 vertices and meets every A_i in exactly one point (|A_i ∩ B_j| = 1), so the k−1 vertices of any B_j cover all of F's sets {A_i} and also every set {x} ∪ T, since T is a transversal of the B_j's. So τ(F) ≤ k−1, which violates the requirement. The stated count is also inconsistent: k−1 disjoint (k−1)-sets have (k−1)^{k−1} transversals, not k^{k−1}. Since the construction fails, the claimed value (k^{k−1}+k−1)² is unsupported.

**Solution B's construction is valid.**
- 𝒢 = k pairwise disjoint k-sets P_1,…,P_k. Any cover must hit every part, so τ(𝒢) = k.
- A k-set meeting all k disjoint parts must contain exactly one vertex from each, so 𝒻 ⊆ {transversals}, giving at most k^k sets. Taking all of them gives |𝒻| = k^k.
- A set C hits every transversal iff some part P_i ⊆ C, so the minimal covers of 𝒻 are exactly the parts. Hence τ(𝒻) = k.

The product is k^k · k = k^{k+1}.

Solution B's comparison with the symmetric construction is also sound: C(2k−1,k)² grows like 16^k, which is smaller than k^{k+1} for large k. I could not fully verify that k^{k+1} is the true maximum, and I'm recalling the literature (Frankl–Kupavskii) only loosely. But B gives a valid construction and A does not, so B is the more likely correct answer.

WINNER: B
